# What this book is {.unnumbered}

This book is the guide to **ISLA** (Invariant Slice Attention), a neural
surrogate for steady, boundary-driven PDE problems: given a discretized
boundary and the problem's global conditions, predict the steady field on
that boundary and in the domain it bounds. It is written the way a user
guide for a design code is written. It teaches what the method computes and
why each part is there, shows how to run it, and then lays out, with the
same care, what the measurements say for it and against it. The reader we
have in mind is fluent in PDE numerics and machine learning and has never
seen this program; every term is defined where it first appears, and every
number is computed, as the page renders, from a checked-in artifact.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the name comes from, and what came before"}
ISLA is pronounced "eye-la". An *isla* is an island: a shape defined
entirely by its boundary, which is what the method takes as input. The code
class is `ISLA` in `physicsnemo.experimental.nn`. An earlier exact-kernel
design of this program, the first MeshTransformer, is documented in the
repository's `book/archive/` directory and does not appear in this book.
:::

## The thesis {#sec-verdict}

**ISLA trades a few percent of in-distribution accuracy for a set of exact
guarantees that no released mesh transformer offers, and the trade is
priced.** Three things are true at once, and the book is organized around
keeping all three in view:

1. **In distribution, the released baselines are slightly more accurate.**
   With every model given the same inputs and scored on the same instrument,
   GeoTransolver and Transolver lead ISLA on every surface benchmark measured
   on the two production aerodynamics datasets, DrivAerML (cars) and
   HiLiftAeroML (wings). The size of the gap depends on how it is measured;
   the table below states it at three resolutions.
2. **ISLA's guarantees are exact and they earn accuracy where they matter.**
   Rotation and translation covariance hold by construction, so when
   geometries arrive in arbitrary poses ISLA leads baselines that learned
   pose from augmentation. Its reference frame reads nothing from the sample,
   so its prediction is consistent under a change of surface sampling where
   every configuration that centres on the sampled points collapses.
3. **The gap has an anatomy.** About half of the headline gap at the
   reference resolution is finite-sample noise that a stratified inference
   draw or more cells removes; about two and a half points are the positional
   information the invariance contracts deny the model; about two points are
   the single-routing form of slice attention. Each part was measured by an
   experiment designed to isolate it (@sec-deficit-anatomy).

```{python}
#| label: setup-index
#| include: false
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
RES = Path("..") / "results"
RP = Path("..") / "research" / "transfer_program" / "studies"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
fp = lambda runs, keys, f="pressure_l2": [runs[k]["fields"][f]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
fpdr = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_drivaer_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
rf = J("relframe_reduction_2026-09-11.json")["drivaer_val"]
qv = J("quadvar_reduction_2026-09-17.json")["arms"]
MAT = J("accuracy_consistency_matrix_2026-09-10.json")
sc = MAT["scale_corner"]["rows"]
cw = J("corner_wlr_reduction_2026-09-15.json")["summary"]
poseB = json.load(open(RP / "campaign_b_pose" / "campaign_b_fp32_2026-09-10.json"))
ri2 = J("relint2_reduction_2026-09-14.json")
eqp = J("eqprice_reduction_2026-09-17.json")["summary"]

gt10 = mean(fp(fpdr, [f"uw_gt_unit_lr1e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)]))
t10 = mean(fp(fpdr, [f"uw_transolver_unit_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)]))
isla10 = mean([rf[f"rf_dr_mt2_meas_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)])
gt_st = mean(qv["gt_unit"]["strat"]["10000"]["seeds"]); t_st = mean(qv["transolver_unit"]["strat"]["10000"]["seeds"])
isla_st = mean(qv["isla_ref"]["strat"]["10000"]["seeds"])
gt_c = sc["geotransolver_unit_512x80k"]["in_family"]; t_c = sc["transolver_unit_512x80k"]["in_family"]
isla_c = mean(cw["in_family_80k_seeds"])
R = MAT["rows"]
dens = {k: R[k]["density_factor"] for k in ("isla_relative_frame_meas", "isla_reference_constant_gauge", "geotransolver_unit", "transolver_unit")}
pose = {"isla": poseB["arms"]["isla"]["pressure_mean"] / poseB["canonical"]["isla"]["pressure_mean"],
        "gt": poseB["arms"]["gt_aug"]["pressure_mean"] / poseB["canonical"]["gt"]["pressure_mean"],
        "t": poseB["arms"]["transolver_aug"]["pressure_mean"] / poseB["canonical"]["transolver_lr3e3"]["pressure_mean"]}
pose_lead = {"gt": poseB["arms"]["gt_aug"]["pressure_mean"] / poseB["arms"]["isla"]["pressure_mean"],
             "t": poseB["arms"]["transolver_aug"]["pressure_mean"] / poseB["arms"]["isla"]["pressure_mean"]}
inter = ri2["ratios_gt_over_relint2"]
pct = lambda r: f"{(1 - r) * 100:.0f}%"
```

The full standing, every rung of both datasets with seeds, paired counts and
artifacts, is the scoreboard of @sec-scoreboard. The HiLiftAeroML rungs are
not in the table above because they tell the same story with larger gaps
at the smallest training sets; @sec-data-efficiency has them.

## The trade in one picture

```{python}
#| label: fig-headline
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The priced trade, on DrivAerML (435 training cars, 48 validation cars,
#|   10,000 cells, float32). Top: in-distribution surface-pressure error,
#|   lower is better; the baselines lead by a few percent. Bottom: how much
#|   each model's error grows when the evaluation departs from the training
#|   conditions, as a factor on a log axis where 1 means unaffected. Filled
#|   bars: the surface is sampled with a 10:1 front-to-back density bias and
#|   each model's input frame is taken from the biased sample. Hatched bars:
#|   every training and validation case is placed in its own random pose;
#|   the baselines were trained with rotation augmentation, ISLA without.
#|   Colours and marks follow the book's key (@fig-key). How to read this:
#|   the top panel is the accuracy ISLA gives up; the bottom panel is what it
#|   buys. It does not show the HiLiftAeroML rungs, the interior task, or the
#|   resolution dependence of the top-panel gap (@tbl-thesis).
#|   Data: as @tbl-thesis.
#| code-fold: true
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 6.2), sharex=True,
                               gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 1.15], hspace=0.12))
keys = ["isla_ref", "isla_cg", "gt", "t"]
names = ["ISLA\nreference", "ISLA\nconstant-gauge variant", "GeoTransolver", "Transolver"]
xs = np.arange(len(keys))
err = [isla10, R["isla_reference_constant_gauge"]["in_family"], gt10, t10]
for x, k, e in zip(xs, keys, err):
    ax0.bar(x, e, width=0.6, **bar_kwargs(k))
    ax0.text(x, e + 0.001, f"{e:.4f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax0.set_ylim(0, 0.07); ax0.set_yticks([0, 0.02, 0.04, 0.06])
ax0.set_ylabel("surface pressure error,\narea-weighted relative L2 [–]")
ax0.set_title("in distribution: lower is better")
ax0.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

dvals = [dens["isla_relative_frame_meas"], dens["isla_reference_constant_gauge"], dens["geotransolver_unit"], dens["transolver_unit"]]
pvals = [None, pose["isla"], pose["gt"], pose["t"]]
w = 0.3
for x, k, d, p in zip(xs, keys, dvals, pvals):
    ax1.bar(x - w / 2, d, width=w, **bar_kwargs(k))
    ax1.text(x - w / 2, d * 1.12, f"{d:.2f}x", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
    if p is not None:
        ax1.bar(x + w / 2, p, width=w, color=STYLE[k]["color"], hatch="///", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
        ax1.text(x + w / 2, p * 1.12, f"{p:.2f}x", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
    else:
        ax1.text(x + w / 2, 1.12, "pose:\nnot run", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7.5, color=MUTED)
ax1.axhline(1.0, color=INK2, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
ax1.set_yscale("log"); ax1.set_ylim(0.8, 30)
ax1.set_yticks([1, 2, 5, 10, 20]); ax1.set_yticklabels(["1", "2", "5", "10", "20"])
ax1.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(mpl.ticker.NullFormatter())
ax1.set_ylabel("error growth when conditions change,\nshifted ÷ in-distribution [–]")
ax1.set_title("out of the training conditions: 1 means unaffected")
ax1.set_xticks(xs); ax1.set_xticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
ax1.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax1.text(3.55, 1.0, " 1 = unaffected", va="center", fontsize=8, color=INK2)
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
ax1.legend(handles=[Patch(facecolor=MUTED, label="10:1 sampling-density bias, sample frame"),
                    Patch(facecolor=MUTED, hatch="///", edgecolor="white", label="every case in a random pose")],
           loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

## Names, symbols and colours {#sec-key}

The book uses one name for each thing and one colour for each architecture.
The names below are canonical; their definitions are in the chapters cited.

| Name | What it is | Where defined |
|---|---|---|
| ISLA, **reference configuration** | the architecture as shipped: relative frame, total-measure length scale, the class default | @sec-mt2 |
| **constant-gauge variant** | ISLA centred on the plain mean of the sampled points with a fixed length unit; behind several early measurements | @sec-mt2-variants |
| **similarity-gauge variant** | ISLA centred on the measure-weighted centroid with the RMS radius as length unit | @sec-mt2-variants |
| **ablation**, **diagnostic** | a configuration measured only to price a design choice (weights-off, raw coordinates); never adopted | @sec-principled-decisions |
| **GeoTransolver**, **Transolver**, **GeoTransolver-volume** | the released slice-attention baselines, never modified; a *research variant* of one carries the surface measure into its pooling to locate a property | @sec-baselines |
| **unit-direction protocol** | every model receives the freestream as a unit vector; the fair-comparison rule that decides the surface ranking | @sec-fair-comparison |
| **global vector / scalar inputs** | the problem's global conditions ($K$ directions, $S$ scalars); here $K = 1$, the freestream direction, and $S = 0$ | @sec-mt2-inputs |
| **measure weight** $w_i$ | the surface area a sampled cell stands for; the quadrature weight of every sum in the model | @sec-mt2-quadrature |
| **slice**, **anchor** | a soft group of tokens, and its measure-weighted mean position and normal | @sec-mt2-slices |
| **relational invariants** | the scalars that describe a token relative to an anchor | @sec-mt2-relational |
| **area-weighted relative L2**, **float32 instrument** | the metric and the precision every reported number is scored at | @sec-metrics |
| **rung** | one training-set size on the data-efficiency ladder ("the 35-case rung") | @sec-data-efficiency |
| **deficit anatomy** | the decomposition of the in-distribution gap into measured parts | @sec-deficit-anatomy |

```{python}
#| label: fig-key
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The book's visual key. Each architecture keeps its hue in every figure;
#|   a variant of an architecture is the same hue at a lighter tint with an
#|   open marker, and an ablation is hatched. Colour is never the only cue:
#|   the marker shape and the line style carry the same distinction.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 2.3))
order = ["isla_ref", "isla_cg", "isla_sg", "isla_abl", "gt", "gt_var", "t", "t_var"]
for i, k in enumerate(order):
    y = -(i % 4); col = i // 4
    x0 = 0.05 + col * 0.5
    kw = series_kwargs(k, lw=2.0, ms=8)
    ax.plot([x0, x0 + 0.08], [y, y], **{a: kw[a] for a in ("color", "ls", "lw")})
    ax.plot([x0 + 0.04], [y], marker=kw["marker"], ms=8, mfc=kw["mfc"], mec=kw["mec"], mew=1.8, ls="none", color=kw["color"])
    if STYLE[k]["hatch"]:
        ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Rectangle((x0 + 0.10, y - 0.3), 0.04, 0.6, **bar_kwargs(k)))
    ax.text(x0 + 0.16, y, STYLE[k]["label"], va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(-3.6, 0.6)
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_aspect("auto")
plt.show()
```

Two conventions hold in every table and figure. **A ratio between
architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error**, so a value above
one favours ISLA. **Every error is the area-weighted relative L2 of
@sec-metrics, scored in float32** on the final-epoch checkpoint; no
bfloat16 number appears in the book.

## How to read this book {#sec-how-to-read}

The book is in five parts and reads in order; each part assumes only the
ones before it.

- **Part I, the problem** (@sec-problem). What a boundary-to-field surrogate
  is, taught on a two-dimensional airfoil whose exact solution we know; the
  two production datasets and their splits; the metric; the frozen protocol.
- **Part II, the architecture.** @sec-mt2 builds ISLA one idea at a time,
  from "a sum over cells should be an integral" to the equivariant output
  basis, with a figure for each idea and the derivations folded away. @sec-baselines
  describes GeoTransolver and Transolver and the fair-comparison rules.
- **Part III, using ISLA** (@sec-using). The configurations and when to use
  each, the inputs the model accepts, the recipe commands, the width
  learning-rate rule, the inference sampler, checkpoints and cost.
- **Part IV, evidence.** @sec-scoreboard is the standing on one page. Behind
  it: data efficiency on the wings (@sec-data-efficiency); accuracy at full
  data, robustness and the deficit anatomy (@sec-full-data); interior
  prediction (@sec-interior).
- **Part V, limits and status.** @sec-limits states the limit of each claim
  and what would move it. @sec-program-status is the live research tech tree.
- **Appendices.** The design-decision ledger (@sec-principled-decisions), and
  the dated lab notebook (@sec-notebook): every preregistration, launch and
  verdict, including the failures, in the order they happened.

Optional depth sits in collapsed notes like the one at the top of this
page. The throughline reads completely with all of them closed.

## What this book does not claim {#sec-not-claimed}

- **Not that ISLA is more accurate in distribution.** On the surface task the
  released baselines lead on every rung measured (@sec-scoreboard). Comparisons
  against baselines fed the physical freestream velocity measure the
  protocol's input scale, not the architectures, and appear only as such
  (@sec-part-baseline).
- **Not that equivariance is an accuracy edge on posed data in general.** A
  baseline trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at about a
  percent of cost (@sec-pose). ISLA's pose lead is against baselines that learn
  pose from augmentation, in random poses.
- **Not that sampling consistency is an invariance.** It is a fine-mesh-limit
  property: the reference frame's small degradation under a 10:1 bias is a
  10,000-cell statement, and on the wings at a fixed angle the bar is not yet
  met at 40,000 cells (@sec-consistency-bench).
- **Not that the interior lead is unconditional.** It is on velocity only, and
  the interacting decode requires at least the training count of points to be
  queried together (@sec-interior-companion).
- **Not that either architecture extrapolates across a flow regime** or
  transfers zero-shot to a different vehicle family (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Not that the HiLift figures are test-set figures.** They are validation
  figures on final-epoch checkpoints; the sealed test was spent on regime
  extrapolation (@sec-limits-validation).
